title: Two kinds of attention
hook: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises (Lutz et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, wandering isn't all bad: the drifting mind can plan and find answers, especially when it knows it's drifting. Your line was wander on purpose. Did a stuck problem come loose? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

A camera has two ways of seeing. Zoom in, and one face fills the frame, sharp, every eyelash, while the background melts away. Pull back to the wide shot, and the whole street is there at once: the bus, the pigeons, the woman with the umbrella, nothing in particular in focus and everything in view. Neither is the right way. They're different tools. A group of researchers looking at meditation described it in terms of the same two shots.
screen: `ZOOM IN: ONE FACE.` → `PULL BACK: THE WHOLE STREET.` → `TWO SHOTS, TWO TOOLS.`

segments.voice: Antoine Lutz, Heleen Slagter, John Dunne and Richard Davidson wrote a paper on attention in meditation, and they described two broad styles. The first they called focused attention. You choose one object, the breath at the nostrils, a sound, a word, and rest there. When the mind wanders, you notice, let go of the distraction, and come back. Sound familiar? It's William James's turn back, done on purpose, again and again. The skills it trains are narrow and strong: holding on, catching the drift, returning. The second they called open monitoring. Here there's no single object. You rest in awareness and notice whatever arises, a sound, an itch, a worry, a memory, without grabbing it and without pushing it away. Then the next thing. Then the next. The skill here is wide: seeing the whole street, and seeing it without reacting. The authors drew on Buddhist practice for these descriptions, and they say these are broad families, not the only kinds of meditation, and that practices can mix them. They also describe focused attention as a common way in: steadying the mind first can make open monitoring easier. Notice how this fits the week. Bringing it back is focused attention. Catching the idling mind, or wandering on purpose and knowing it, comes closer to open monitoring. Both are attention. One narrows the beam. One widens it. And a meditator, like a good photographer, learns when to zoom and when to pull back.
screen: `FOCUSED ATTENTION: ONE OBJECT.` · `CATCH THE DRIFT, COME BACK.` · `OPEN MONITORING: WHATEVER ARISES.` · `FOCUS FIRST, THEN OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try each, about a minute apiece. Settle. First, focus. Choose the breath at the nostrils and rest there. When the mind drifts, notice, and come back. Then, at about the halfway point, open. Let go of the breath as an anchor. Notice whatever shows up: a sound, a sensation, a thought. Let each one come and go, like people crossing a wide street. Don't follow any of them. Just watch. The bell holds the time.
Two kinds of attention. Focused attention rests on one object and returns to it; open monitoring watches whatever arises without grabbing. Today's word.
Your line: focus, then open. Today, on one walk or one wait, spend a minute zoomed in on a single thing, then pull back and take in the whole scene. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Some meditation teachers begin students with focused attention on the breath to steady the mind, then introduce open awareness of whatever arises; researchers study the two styles separately because they seem to train different skills.

fork.setup: you're sitting, and a car alarm goes off down the street. you're practicing open monitoring. what do you do?
options: shut it out and return hard to the breath.
notice the sound, let it come and go, and keep watching.
get up and see whose car it is.
fork.reveal: in open monitoring there's no single object to defend. the alarm is simply the next thing that arises, noticed without grabbing.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation is one thing: clearing the mind.
what it means: there are at least two broad styles. focused attention narrows the beam onto one object. open monitoring widens it to whatever arises.

what a scholar hears: Lutz, Slagter, Dunne and Davidson's distinction between focused attention and open monitoring, drawn from Buddhist practice, which lets researchers study each style's effects separately.

sources.ref: Lutz, A., Slagter, H. A., Dunne, J. D., and Davidson, R. J., Attention regulation and monitoring in meditation, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 12 (2008)
